blocks.text: Until 1928, Turkish was written in the Ottoman script, a form of the Arabic alphabet used across the Ottoman Empire for centuries. It served Arabic and Persian words well, but not Turkish sounds. Turkish has eight vowels, and the script had only a few letters for vowels, which writers often left out, so the same written word could be read in several ways.

Reformers had debated the script since the 19th century. In June 1928, a language commission (*Dil Encümeni*) began meeting in Ankara to design a Latin alphabet fitted to Turkish. In August, at an evening event in Gülhane Park in Istanbul, Mustafa Kemal, the president of the Republic and later known as Atatürk, presented the new letters. In the weeks that followed he toured the country and taught them in person, chalk in hand at a blackboard.

The Grand National Assembly passed the law on the new Turkish letters on 1 November 1928, and it came into force two days later. The deadlines were short: newspapers, magazines and signs had to switch by 1 December 1928, and state offices, banks and new books by 1 January 1929. Petitions written in the old script were accepted only until June 1929.

The new alphabet had 29 letters, one for each sound of Turkish. It left out q, w and x and brought in letters such as *ç*, *ş*, *ğ*, *ö*, *ü* and the dotless *ı*. The aim was a spelling so regular that anyone who knows the letters can read any word aloud: the skill you practise in this unit.

Adults had to learn to read too. From 1 January 1929, the Nation's Schools (*Millet Mektepleri*) ran short reading and writing courses all over the country, and more than a million people enrolled in the first year. At the 1927 census, about one person in ten could read; by the 1935 census, about one in five.

blocks.title: Teachers' Day
blocks.text: On 24 November 1928, Mustafa Kemal accepted the title of *Başöğretmen*, head teacher of the Nation's Schools. Since 1981, Turkey has celebrated 24 November as Teachers' Day (*Öğretmenler Günü*).

The reform is still discussed. Supporters point to how quickly reading spread once spelling became simple. Critics note that it cut later generations off from centuries of books and documents in the old script, which today mostly specialists read.
Imagine the first lesson at a Nation's School in January 1929. With the phrases from this unit, you can already read how a teacher might have begun:

blocks.tr: Günaydın, hoş geldiniz! Benim adım Ayşe. Memnun oldum.
blocks.en: Good morning, welcome! My name is Ayşe. Nice to meet you.
